context: The input is choices = [4, 4, 5] at indices 0, 1, and 2. “First 4” and “second 4” distinguish indices 0 and 1. The figure marks the second 4 with a hat. Both have value 4. Subset sum II permits each index at most once and requires distinct solutions. To show the problem with equal candidates, the figure initially follows subset sum I: start = i in the next round, allowing reuse of the current index.
description: At the top is the array choices. A partial two-level search tree starts empty. The first round chooses the first 4, the second 4, or 5. Only the branch [first 4, …] expands in the second round, trying all three candidates. In both rounds, the third branch is labeled only +5, with no prefix shown.

One gray arc connects [first 4, …] and [second 4, …]. Another connects [first 4, first 4, …] and [first 4, second 4, …]. Both are labeled “Duplicate subsets.” The first pair shares the numerical prefix [4, …], and the second pair shares [4, 4, …]. Choosing the first 4 again also reuses index 0, which subset sum II forbids.

frames.explanation: To avoid duplicates in subset sum II, prevent reuse of an index on the same path and try each distinct value only once per round. The two 4s at different indices can still be chosen in successive rounds.
frames.title: Equal candidates introduce duplicate combinations

summary: Two candidates with value 4 can produce branches with identical subset contents when tried in the same round.
title: Equal candidates introduce duplicate combinations
